From Moot Court Memorials to Constitutional Realities: Decoding State of Haryana v. Prakash Chopra 

Where exactly do we draw the line between rooting out corruption and protecting personal liberty in the digital age? Wrestling with this exact dilemma over the past few weeks while researching and drafting memorials for the 14th RGNUL National Moot Court Competition, 2026 has been nothing short of an eye-opener. 
The case throws you right into the deep end of criminal law touching everything from whether employees of a private school can be tried as "public servants", to the chaos of unauthorized surveillance, biometric lock-picking on phones, and crypto wallets. 
Some of the most gripping questions we had to tackle included that 
The "Public Servant" Debate - Does a private school staff member cross into the territory of the Prevention of Corruption Act just because the institution got a land concession and has to follow state regulations? 
Privacy vs. Truth - Should courts admit crucial evidence even if it was snatched through deeply questionable or illegal police methods, or does constitutional morality demand its outright exclusion? 
Your Mind vs. Your Device - Is forcing someone to cough up a laptop password or biometrically unlock their phone a violation of the right against self-incrimination Article 20(3), or is it just fetching a digital key to physical evidence? 
The Sanction Trap - What happens when sections 17-A and 19 require prior sanction, but the internal authorities who are supposed to grant it might have conflicts of interest themselves? 
Looking at how century-old constitutional doctrines have to bend, stretch and adapt to modern tech like encrypted messaging and crypto assets really changes how you view criminal jurisprudence.
Curious to hear from fellow mooters and tech-law enthusiasts how would you balance the state's fight against corruption with absolute digital privacy? Let’s chat in the comments!
